clinicalPearls: A rare condition of recurrent episodes of painless upper eyelid oedema, typically beginning in youth
Repeated attacks stretch and thin the eyelid skin, leaving redundant, atrophic, crinkled tissue
It is distinct from dermatochalasis, which is age-related redundant lid skin without inflammatory episodes
Chronic changes can include ptosis, lacrimal gland prolapse and fat atrophy or herniation
It usually affects the upper lids and may be unilateral or bilateral
Surgery is deferred until the disease has quiesced, as operating during active swelling gives poor results
reference.pathophysiology: Blepharochalasis is characterised by recurrent bouts of eyelid angio-oedema-like swelling of uncertain cause, thought to involve localised inflammation with elastolysis. Repeated inflammatory episodes degrade elastic fibres in the eyelid skin, producing progressive atrophy, laxity and thinning, and can weaken the levator aponeurosis and orbital septum, leading to ptosis, fat herniation and prolapse of the lacrimal gland. The condition tends to enter a quiescent phase in later life once the acute episodes subside.
additionalDifferentials: Cutis laxa or other elastic-tissue disorder
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the history of recurrent painless lid swelling
Documentation of episodes and resulting lid changes
Exclusion of allergic, thyroid and systemic causes of lid oedema
Assessment of levator function and lacrimal gland position
Photography to monitor progression and quiescence
redFlags: Features suggesting an alternative systemic cause of recurrent oedema
Functional visual impairment from ptosis or dermatochalasis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but episodes can recur for years before quiescence; surgical correction of the residual deformity gives good results once the disease is inactive.
pitfalls: Confusing it with simple age-related dermatochalasis
Overlooking associated ptosis or lacrimal gland prolapse
Failing to exclude allergic or systemic causes of lid oedema
management: Defer surgical intervention until the disease has entered a quiescent phase, as operating during active swelling gives poor results
Exclude allergic, thyroid and systemic causes of recurrent eyelid oedema during active episodes
Monitor episodes and progression with serial documentation and photography

Once quiescent, surgically correct the residual deformity with blepharoplasty and excision of redundant atrophic skin, levator aponeurosis repair for ptosis and repositioning of a prolapsed lacrimal gland
Reassure the patient that the condition is benign and tends to settle in later life
Refer to oculoplastic surgery for assessment and reconstruction
